chapters.title: Chapter 4: Strategy Sensitivity and Break-Even Analysis

lessons.title: Case Study: Comparing Cost Drag Across a Daily and a Monthly Rebalance Strategy

children.text: This case study puts every tool from this chapter to work on one decision: the same alpha signal, tested at two different rebalance frequencies. It is also, in disguise, the same trap Chapter 1 warned about, a higher gross return winning a comparison it should not win, now worked through with the exact formulas this chapter built.
The Setup: Same Signal, Two Rebalance Frequencies

A value-momentum composite signal is backtested on a 30-stock portfolio drawn from the Nifty 200, two ways. Version A rebalances daily, reacting to every change in the signal as fast as possible. Version B rebalances monthly, accepting that its signal is somewhat stale between rebalances in exchange for trading far less. Both share the same underlying alpha logic and the same 0.30% blended round-trip cost established earlier in this course.
Step 1: The Gross Backtest Looks Like an Easy Choice

Reacting to every signal change, Version A's gross backtest shows an 18% CAGR. Version B, slower to respond, shows a lower 14% gross CAGR. On gross returns alone, Version A wins comfortably, and this is exactly the comparison Chapter 1 warned would mislead an optimizer that never looks past gross numbers.
Step 2: Apply the Cost Drag Formula

body.caption: Gross CAGR, cost drag, and net CAGR for both versions

body.title: Gross vs Net CAGR: Daily vs Monthly Rebalance

body.text: The ranking completely inverts. On gross returns, A beats B by 4 points. On net returns, B beats A by more than 6 points, because A's far higher turnover multiplies the same round-trip cost more than twelve times as often as B's does. This is Chapter 1 Lesson 3's flat-haircut trap made concrete: a cost-blind comparison would have picked the wrong strategy with total confidence.

children.text: Step 3: Apply the Break-Even Safety Margin

Net CAGR alone still understates how different these two strategies actually are. Divide each version's gross CAGR by its own break-even gross CAGR, its cost drag, to see how much of a safety margin each one is really running on.

body.caption: Safety margin: gross CAGR versus break-even gross CAGR

body.text: Version A clears break-even, technically, but at a 1.6x margin, below the 2x to 3x guideline from Lesson 3. Given that this course has repeatedly shown real-world costs running higher than modeled, Chapter 1's market impact miss, Chapter 3's underestimated slippage, a 1.6x margin offers very little room for the cost model to be even slightly wrong before Version A turns net-negative live. Version B's 15.6x margin has room to absorb a badly wrong cost estimate and still come out ahead.

children.text: Version B is the strategy worth taking live: higher net CAGR, and a safety margin nearly ten times more comfortable than Version A's. Version A's headline 18% gross CAGR, the number that would win a naive comparison, was never the number that mattered. Everything this chapter built, turnover, holding period, cost drag, break-even, and margin of safety, exists to make sure that number never gets to make the decision on its own again.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Version A had the higher gross CAGR (18% vs 14%) but the lower net CAGR (6.75% vs 13.10%) and the thinner safety margin (1.6x vs 15.6x). What is the single best explanation for why Version A performed worse on every cost-aware measure despite its stronger gross number?
options: Version A's underlying alpha signal was fundamentally weaker than Version B's
Version A's far higher turnover (37.5x vs 3.0x) multiplied the same round-trip cost many more times per year, consuming most of its larger gross edge
Version B used a cheaper broker than Version A
Version A's backtest period was shorter than Version B's
body.explanation: Both versions shared the same signal, universe, and round-trip cost assumption. The only structural difference was turnover, 37.5x versus 3.0x, more than twelve times as much. Cost drag scales directly with turnover, so Version A's larger gross edge was overwhelmed by a proportionally much larger cost drag.

body.text: A higher gross CAGR is not a reason to prefer a strategy, and this case study shows exactly how badly that instinct can fail: the strategy with the lower gross return won decisively on net CAGR and on safety margin, purely because its turnover was more than twelve times lower. Rebalance frequency is a design choice with real economic consequences, not a neutral implementation detail.

points: Given the same signal and universe, Version A (daily rebalance, 37.5x turnover) showed an 18% gross CAGR against Version B's (monthly rebalance, 3.0x turnover) 14%, but the ranking fully inverted on net CAGR: 6.75% versus 13.10%.
Version A's safety margin over its own break-even gross CAGR was only 1.6x, below this chapter's 2x to 3x guideline, while Version B's was 15.6x, comfortably above it.
Comparing strategies on gross returns alone, exactly the trap named in Chapter 1, would have selected the objectively worse strategy on every cost-aware measure.
Rebalance frequency should be treated as a first-class design decision with a direct, quantifiable cost consequence, not an implementation detail decided after the alpha signal is chosen.
